title: Talking Is Also Thinking
author: Zia Hassan
summary: Zia Hassan, a PhD student at Johns Hopkins, describes how he responded to AI-written essays in his community college Education 101 class. After a detector mistook a well-written essay for AI output, he concluded that blue books, bans, and oral exams were short-sighted and instead stopped trying to catch students. He moved to ungrading, pass or fail with unlimited revision, and added peer coaching: paired students spend ten to fifteen minutes each asking the other open, probing questions about the essay prompt, then ask for a takeaway and a commitment to a concrete next action. He says students arrive at the draft with their own thinking and less temptation to use an LLM, and their work shows greater depth. He ties the approach to research that grades act as extrinsic motivators, and gives steps for trying it plus a starter list of powerful questions.
points: Peer coaching pairs students for a pre-draft conversation in which the coach only asks probing questions and never offers advice.
Each session ends with a takeaway and a commitment to a specific next action, which creates a built-in accountability partner.
Students who have already explored their own ideas are less inclined to hand drafting to an LLM and write with greater depth.
Ungrading with complete-or-not-yet marks and unlimited revisions removes the grade incentive that drives much AI shortcutting.
Teachers should model a real coaching session, supply powerful questions, and rescue stuck pairs by suggesting a question.
quotes: People say that writing is thinking, and that’s absolutely true. But talking is also thinking, and it’s something students rarely get to do.
In that moment, I knew educators everywhere were in for a bumpy ride. The classroom experience would have to change. And quickly.

Peer coaching is a structure that enables students to probe one another to think more deeply about a topic, motivate them to integrate their unique perspective, and help them to commit to a next action.
Instead of sending students home to write the first draft of an essay, I instead pair them up in class for what is almost a pre-draft.

The biggest change I’ve seen in their work is depth. Their essays aren’t necessarily longer, and they don’t necessarily cover new topics, but because they’ve had time to really dive into the topic, the depth of their thinking has dramatically increased.
The most common reason students turn to a generative AI tool is that they want a good grade. If grades are the main currency, students will always look for ways to maximize them with minimal effort.

Using peer coaching allows us to design for growth instead of grades. Hopefully, if we use techniques like this to motivate students to invest in their growth, we won’t have to fight AI shortcuts. Students simply won’t want to take them.
